newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's ANC plays down violent rhetoric of past.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's ANC plays down violent rhetoric of past.

text.p: South Africa's ruling African National Congress (ANC) played down its past violent rhetoric on Tuesday, portraying chants such as "Kill the boer, kill the farmer" as an art form not a statement of policy.

Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told a hearing of Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission that the chants, and magazine and radio reports, calling for the elimination of whites or Zulu foes were merely rhetoric.

Commissioner Howard Vally asked Mbeki about the chant "Kill the boer, kill the farmer", which ANC youth leader Peter Mokaba -- now deputy minister of tourism and environmental affairs -- repeated at campaign rallies for the 1994 democratic elections.
Vally said four people convicted of murder had applied to the commission for amnesty on the grounds that their actions had been motivated by the chant.
Mbeki responded that only people who did not understand African culture would regard the chant as a policy statement.
"This is not a statement," he said. "In Xhosa, this is a form of art. It would not be read by African youth as a statement."
Leading a high-level ANC delegation to the hearing, Mbeki insisted that the party had never regarded the Inkatha Freedom Party of Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi as a military enemy.

On Monday, Mbeki told the commission the ANC leadership had rejected a proposal to kill Buthelezi -- now home affairs minister in the government of national unity -- which was put forward by a unit in KwaZulu-Natal province during the war against apartheid.
About 15,000 people were killed in a decade of violence between Inkatha and the ANC that erupted in the mid-1980s.
Mbeki said the violence was provoked by the white government which had the "foolish perception" that the ANC represented the Xhosa tribe while Inkatha represented Zulus.

"There was this thesis among white intelligence officers... 'We need to make sure they do not get together or you will have permanent one-party domination in this country forever and forever'," Mbeki said.
Members of the commission asked about articles in ANC magazines during the 1980s which described Buthelezi and Inkatha as enemies who should be eliminated.
Mbeki replied that this kind of denunciation was common between political rivals. "It's not in the nature of political parties to be complimentary about each other," he said.

Mathews Phosa, a senior member of the ANC delegation, said that to claim amnesty on the basis of the chant was the same as trying to excuse as a political crime the rape of a woman related to an apartheid official.
Buthelezi said in a radio interview on Tuesday he was not surprised to hear there was a suggestion that he be killed, and said he believed there were several such ANC plots against him.
Asked about this by the commission, Mbeki said the apartheid-era secret services had fed Buthelezi misinformation aimed at ensuring there was no rapprochement with the ANC.
Mbeki said the violence was orchestrated by a network of police, magistrates, white right-wingers and Zulu "warlords" which was set up early in the 1980s.
He said the network probably still existed and urged the commission to try to expose it.
